blocks.text: **The problem.** Sort an array of integers `nums` in **ascending** order, **in place**, in O(n log n) time — using a heap.

blocks.alt: Heap sort keeps the array in two parts: a max-heap at the front and the sorted values at the back. Each round moves the heap's top, the largest value left, to the front of the sorted part, until the heap is empty.

elements.text: each round: swap the top to the end of the heap, shrink it, sift down
elements.originalText: each round: swap the top to the end of the heap, shrink it, sift down

blocks.text: Find the **largest** value in the unsorted part, swap it to the end, and shrink the unsorted part by one. Repeat. It's simple, in place — and slow, because finding the largest takes a full scan every round.

**Time O(n²), space O(1).** Heap sort is exactly this idea, with one change: keep the unsorted part in a **max-heap**, so the largest value is always at index 0 instead of somewhere you have to search for.
2. Optimal: pop everything from a min-heap
Put all the values in a min-heap — building it at once is O(n) — then pop n times. Values come out smallest first, already sorted.

blocks.code:
import heapq

def heap_sort(nums):
    heap = list(nums)
    heapq.heapify(heap)                          # build a min-heap in O(n)
    return [heapq.heappop(heap) for _ in range(len(heap))]   # smallest first

blocks.text: **Time O(n log n), space O(n)** for the heap and the output. Fast, but not in place — the problem asks for O(1) extra space.
The key idea: the heap and the sorted part share one array

Build a **max-heap** in place with bottom-up heapify (the last lesson). Its largest value is at index 0 — and it belongs at the **end** of the array. So **swap** it with the last value of the heap, **shrink** the heap by one, and **sift down** the value that just landed on top. The heap shrinks from the right while the sorted part grows into the space it leaves behind.

blocks.alt: Sorting 5, 2, 9, 1, 6, 3. Phase 1 builds the max-heap 9, 6, 5, 1, 2, 3. Round 1 swaps 9 to the end and sifts 3 down: 6, 3, 5, 1, 2, then 9 sorted. Round 2 swaps 6 to the end and sifts 2 down: 5, 3, 2, 1, then 6, 9 sorted. After the last round the array reads 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9.

blocks.text: **Time O(n log n), space O(1).** Building is O(n); then n − 1 rounds each sift down at most log n levels. Unlike quicksort, there's no bad pivot: heap sort is O(n log n) **in the worst case**, with no extra memory.

Two catches. It's **not stable** — equal values can change their order, because the swap to the end jumps over everything in between. And it jumps around the array, which makes it slower in practice than quicksort or merge sort, which read memory in order.

items: **Empty array** and **one value** — both loops do nothing.
**Already sorted** and **reverse sorted** — still O(n log n), no slow case.
**All equal** — `[4, 4, 4]`: no swaps change anything; use `>`, not `>=`, when picking a child.
**Sort in descending order** — build a **min**-heap instead: the smallest values move to the end.
**Partial sort: the k largest in order** — stop after k rounds; the last k slots hold them, sorted. O(n + k log n).
**Kth Largest Element in an Array** — the same rounds, stopped at the kth. In the interview questions below.
**Sort a nearly sorted (k-sorted) array** — a heap of size k + 1 sorts it in O(n log k). Also below.
